transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-19 15:00 PST / Duration 75 minutes / Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark Chen (CTO, Ironclad), Leah Ortiz (Head of Security), Darius Patel (Infra)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh, appreciate the time. We're here to walk through the security architecture for Redwood Private in a VPC/on-prem pattern, and to make sure it meets Ironclad's controls. Priya and Samir will do most of the technical details. Mark, Leah, Darius, sound good?

[00:12] Mark: Yep sounds good. We have a pretty strict set of controls around egress and key management so eager to hear details.

[00:20] Priya: Great. Quick agenda: high level deployment modes, the VPC network layout we recommend, ingress and egress patterns, firewalling and IPS/IDS options, key management with KMS or HSM, RBAC and SSO integration, audit logs and retention, and then Q&A. I'll start with high level.

[01:05] Priya: So Redwood Private is deployed into customer-managed VPCs. We support two main network patterns: 1) VPC peering / transit gateway where the Redwood nodes sit in a customer VPC isolated subnets and communicate over private routes; 2) AWS PrivateLink (or cloud provider equivalent) where control-plane traffic is via interface endpoints. Both support no-internet egress for inference plane if you configure NAT and route tables appropriately.

[01:42] Leah: Can you clarify "no-internet egress"? We require zero direct internet egress from inference nodes. All outbound must go through our egress firewall and proxy.

[01:52] Priya: Yes. You can place Redwood instances in private subnets with no internet gateway attached; route outbound to a NAT instance or egress appliance that you control. Alternatively, you can use VPC endpoints for S3/KMS etc so traffic never traverses internet. We also support putting the control plane in a separate management VPC with peering and very limited ports.

[02:20] Darius: And what about OS-level access? We prefer to avoid bastion hosts if possible.

[02:25] Samir: You can use session-manager (SSM) style access or an ephemeral jump with approved bastion that has strict security groups. We also ship an ops container that only listens on localhost unless you enable SSH for debugging; default pattern is no SSH access for infra.

[03:05] Priya: On firewalling: we recommend a layered approach. Security groups for host-level allow lists, NACLs for subnet-level restrictions, route tables to limit egress, and per-tenant security policies inside Redwood runtime to restrict model access. For example, lock down outbound to only your KMS endpoint, your artifact S3 buckets, and internal telemetry endpoints.

[03:40] Mark: How do you prevent data exfil via model responses or telemetry? We need to make sure generated tokens are not sent outside our audit path.

[03:50] Priya: Good question. We support explicit outbound allow-listing. Telemetry can be configured to route to a customer-managed endpoints. Also, we offer a "no-telemetry" mode where logs are stored locally and shipped to your ingestion pipeline. For generated outputs, the inference plane only returns responses to the client IPs we see in the VPC or via PrivateLink; you can pair that with egress firewall rules and DLP appliances.

[04:30] Leah: We also require audit logging with tamper-evidence and retention for 7 years. How do you handle audit logs and immutability?

[04:40] Priya: We push audit logs to customer-owned S3 buckets via VPC endpoints and recommend S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for immutability. We also support pushing to your SIEM via Kinesis or Kafka in the VPC. Logs include request metadata, model version, token counts (aggregated), and admin actions. Note that some low-level kernel logs remain on instances and need to be forwarded; our agents can ship these securely.

[05:25] Darius: About KMS: do you integrate with customer KMS and HSM? We need keys to be under our control.

[05:33] Priya: Yes we integrate with customer-managed KMS. We support AWS KMS with customer CMKs and HSM-backed keys, as well as Vault and cloud provider KMS equivalents. Keys are only referenced, not exported. We also support per-tenant envelope encryption and rotate keys on customer schedule.

[06:05] Mark: Does Redwood store any plaintext data in your control plane?

[06:09] Jordan: Short answer no, for Private deployments the control plane can be run in your VPC and we don't retain user data. For hosted we have strict data retention policies. For Private, all data storage can be provisioned into your buckets or DBs.

[06:30] Leah: What about RBAC and SSO? We need SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning and role separation.

[06:36] Priya: We support SAML 2.0 SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. We map SAML roles to RBAC roles in Redwood Console (admin, operator, auditor). You can enforce MFA via your IdP. Audit trail includes who called what API keys were used (we support per-user and per-service keys).

[07:10] Darius: What about secret management — where do API keys live?

[07:15] Samir: API keys are stored encrypted with your KMS. You can enable short-lived tokens with our STS integration so keys are ephemeral and rotated automatically. For long-lived keys, we recommend storing in your secret manager and referencing them via IAM roles.

[07:45] Mark: Network segmentation question: we have multiple teams in one account. Can we host multiple Redwood tenant clusters in the same VPC but isolated?

[07:55] Priya: Yes, we recommend per-tenant subnets and security groups. The runtime supports namespace-level isolation with network policies and per-namespace IAM roles. For stronger isolation we recommend separate VPCs with transit gateway.

[08:28] Leah: Egress controls — do you support egress filtering with an allow-list for external domains?

[08:34] Priya: We support egress allow-listing at the host level and you can pair with your network firewall / egress proxy. Typical pattern: all instances route to egress appliance that does TLS inspection and domain allow-listing. We recommend terminating TLS at the proxy in your VPC. If you need TLS preservation, then you can use mTLS between Redwood and allowed services.

[09:05] Darius: Are there recommended ports and protocols we need to open between our services and Redwood nodes?

[09:12] Samir: Minimal set: control-plane port 8443 (control API), metrics/telemetry endpoints on 9100/9090 optionally, and model-serving ports we expose on localhost by default; if you expose to other subnets we use configured ports. We'll share a full port list in the deployment checklist.

[09:40] Priya: On IDS/IPS: you can plug in your managed IDS via VPC traffic mirroring or host-level agents. We have optional integrations with major IDS vendors. We also emit audit events for any admin API calls.

[10:15] Mark: How do you handle patching? We need cadence and proof of patch levels for SOC2.

[10:21] Samir: For Private we provide AMI/images with a patch cadence defined in SLA — default monthly patching, emergency patches as needed. We produce SBOM and CVE reports per image and can integrate with your vulnerability scanner.

[10:50] Leah: For SOC2 evidence, can you provide Type II report and pen-test summaries?

[10:55] Jordan: Yes, we'll share SOC2 Type II report excerpts relevant to the Private deployment and summaries of third-party pen-tests. Action item: share SOC2 report redacted for public sensitive info.

[11:20] Priya: Now a quick diagram walkthrough — I'm going to describe a sample architecture: Customer VPC A contains Redwood worker subnets (private), internal ELB or NLB for internal traffic, route to egress appliance, endpoints to S3 and KMS via VPC endpoints. Control plane in management VPC B with peered routes limited to specific control IPs. Identity lives in your IdP; admin traffic from console uses SAML to authenticate.

[12:15] [Priya screenshare references diagram link: https://redwood.docs/diagrams/private-vpc-sample.png]

[12:28] Darius: If we use PrivateLink vs peering, what's the tradeoff?

[12:33] Priya: PrivateLink gives you interface endpoints, which are easier for cross-account isolation and don't require route table changes across many VPCs. Peering/transit gateway is lower-latency and may be cheaper at scale but requires more route management. PrivateLink is a good fit if you want to lock down control plane to a small set of endpoints.

[13:05] Mark: About DNS and split-horizon: we have internal-only DNS zones. Does Redwood respect client DNS settings?

[13:12] Samir: Yes you can configure the nodes to use VPC DNS resolvers and we support conditional forwarding. For PrivateLink we expose internal DNS names mapped to the interface endpoints.

[13:40] Leah: Any considerations about data residency? Our regulators require certain customer data never leave AWS region us-east-2.

[13:48] Priya: We support region-pinning for both control and inference planes; for Private deployments the nodes are deployed in your region only. We'll include region-specific AMIs and no cross-region replication unless you explicitly enable it.

[14:15] Darius: Let's drill into firewalling specifics. We want to block ephemeral outbound connections from containers — how do you enforce that?

[14:22] Priya: At the host level we run the runtime as a service user and use eBPF-based network policies and iptables rules to control container egress. We also enforce per-workload policies in the runtime that only allow connections to configured endpoints. If you need stricter controls, you can run sidecar proxies.

[15:00] Mark: For compliance we need full request/response logs including model version. How big are those logs and retention impact?

[15:06] Priya: Request metadata is lightweight; storing full token streams for high volume is expensive. We recommend sampling or storing token hashes unless regulators require full content retention. We can provide options: metadata-only, metadata+redacted output, or full output. We'll size retention estimates in the benchmark.

[15:40] Leah: We also need an offline forensic copy in a WORM bucket for certain incident response workflows.

[15:45] Priya: We can push a daily snapshot to your WORM S3 with object lock. That satisfies many forensic requirements.

[16:10] Samir: Quick note on model artifacts: model weights can be encrypted at rest with your KMS and stored in your private artifact repo. The runtime mounts them but never leaves them unencrypted on disk — ephemeral scratch is encrypted too.

[16:40] Darius: Pen testing: do you allow us to run internal pen-tests against Redwood nodes?

[16:45] Jordan: Yes we have a pen-test coordinate flow; you'll file an auth form, scope the IPs and the testing windows. We'll provide a contact and we require notify prior to tests for production vs staging.

[17:10] Priya: Now let's talk about network diagrams for integration: we'll need your VPC CIDRs, a list of allowed outbound endpoints, and the IdP metadata for SAML. Darius, you mentioned you can share that — we'll need it as an action item.

[17:35] Darius: Yep I'll gather and send.

[17:42] Leah: A couple more questions: 1) Are there any managed services Redwood calls out to that would require extra approvals? 2) Does any telemetry leave our VPC to Redwood-managed endpoints?

[17:55] Priya: For Private deployments, telemetry can be configured to go to customer endpoints only. There are optional Redwood-admin portals that if you opt-in may touch Redwood control plane. We can default to fully customer-owned telemetry. Managed services like image registries can be your own or ours; we recommend pushing images to your ECR.

[18:28] Mark: Competitors question: we've looked at BigCloudAI and EdgeServe. One of our concerns with them was noisy egress and unclear key ownership. How is Redwood different?

[18:36] Jordan: Our differentiator for Private is customer-managed keys, region pinning, and a deployment mode where we don't control egress. We'll share the SOC2 artifacts that specifically call out segregation for Private deployments.

[19:05] Priya: Ok next I'll go over a short checklist we provide for the initial pilot: VPC CIDRs, security group templates, KMS key ARNs, SAML metadata, sample workload, and target SLOs for latency/cost.

[19:30] [Screen reference: deployment-checklist.xlsx link provided]

[19:40] Darius: On SLOs — we expect sub-200ms p95 for our 1K token prompt workload. Can you commit to that in Private?

[19:48] Priya: We'll need to run a benchmark with your exact model and sequence lengths; typical 1 GPU config can meet that with right batching and cache. We'll run a mini-benchmark as next step.

[20:10] Leah: Any encryption at transit recommendations? We require mTLS for all inter-service comms.

[20:16] Samir: We support mTLS inside the VPC for service-to-service, and TLS for external endpoints. For PrivateLink endpoints we recommend mTLS and client certs can be issued by your PKI.

[20:45] Jordan: To wrap up, let's restate action items and next steps. Priya will send network diagram, deployment checklist, and SOC2 redacted report. Priya will also schedule and run the benchmark. Jordan will send pricing. Darius will share VPC details and IdP metadata.

[21:10] Mark: Sounds good. Appreciate the clear path forward.

[21:15] Leah: A couple quick clarifications: can you confirm that S3 endpoints will be via VPC endpoint and not over public internet?

[21:22] Priya: Confirm - VPC endpoints only. We'll include that in the diagram.

[21:30] Jordan: Great. Any last questions?

[21:32] Darius: No, thank you.

[21:35] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and set up the benchmark. End call.

[21:42] [call end]
